s: Part two.
Custom slash commands and skills.
By the end of this part, you'll know how a skill is built, which switches decide who can start it, what its argument and tool fields really do, and how to run it in its own space.
Plain version first.
Some instructions you want read out every shift.
Others you need a few times a month.
Reading those out every shift would be a waste.
For those, you want a procedure card in a labeled drawer.
It's pulled out only when the job calls for it.
And because the card is pulled only when something matches, the label on the drawer does more work than anything written on the card.
The technical name for the card is a skill.
A skill is a folder containing a file called SKILL.md.
That file starts with a short header block called frontmatter, written in a simple key-and-value format.
After that comes the body, which is the actual instructions.
How does a skill get triggered?
Two ways.
A person can type a slash and its name.
That's why skills show up as slash commands.
Or Claude can load it automatically, when it judges the skill relevant.
The description field in the frontmatter is what Claude reads when deciding whether to load it.
So the description is the selection signal.
It's not documentation.
Where do skills live?
The same logic as part one.
Project skills go in .claude/skills/, in a folder named for the skill, holding SKILL.md.
They're committed and shared.
Personal skills go in ~/.claude/skills/.
Only you have them.
Enterprise skills arrive through managed settings.
And plugin skills are namespaced with the plugin name and a colon, so they can't collide.
Now the second source disagreement.
The lesson eleven slide deck treats custom slash commands and skills as two separate features.
The notes, checked against current documentation, say custom commands have merged into skills.
A file at .claude/commands/deploy.md, and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md, both create /deploy.
And they behave the same way.
Command files still work.
They take their name from the file name.
And they accept the same frontmatter, except the name and paths fields, which command files ignore.
What does the skill layout add?
A folder for supporting files, and automatic activation.
So if a question asks you to distinguish them, the honest answer is packaging and automatic activation.
Not capability.
And if a question treats them as separate features, answer in its terms.
Here's a genuinely surprising fact.
And it's a known trap.
When two skills share a name, one has to win.
Why?
Because a lookup by name has to return exactly one thing.
The order is: enterprise beats personal.
And personal beats project.
Your personal skill beats the team's.
That's the opposite of the intuition from CLAUDE.md.
The notes explain why it isn't inconsistent.
Hold on to this line.
A merge never has to choose.
A lookup always does.
Here's the failure story from the notes.
An engineer wrote a personal deploy-staging skill months ago, while prototyping.
It points at a cluster that no longer exists.
Their invocations fail, while everyone else's succeed.
Why?
The stale personal skill silently shadows the committed team skill.
The remedy is to delete or rename the personal file.
Distractors will say the project skill takes precedence.
Or that both skills concatenate, like CLAUDE.md files.
Neither is true.
So remember.
Skills resolve by name, with personal above project.
That's the reverse of how CLAUDE.md behaves.
Question one.
Practice question D3-006.
This one combines scope with the first frontmatter switch.
Here's the scenario.
An engineer built a security audit command in their personal commands folder.
It scans dependencies and opens tickets.
Teammates get command not found.
The team wants three things.
One, available to every contributor.
Two, reviewed in pull requests like other code.
Three, never triggered by Claude on its own initiative, because it creates tickets.
What should they do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Commit it as a project skill.
And set a frontmatter field called disable-model-invocation to true.
Here's the plain version.
It's like keeping the team's fire-drill checklist in your own desk drawer.
It works perfectly for you, and nobody else can find it.
Put it in the shared binder instead.
And mark it: only a manager starts this drill.
That way nobody sets off the alarm by accident.
In exam terms, disable-model-invocation set to true makes the skill user-only.
It runs when a person types the slash command.
Claude will never start it on its own.
That's the right control for anything with side effects.
Now the tempting mirror.
There's another field called user-invocable.
Setting it to false does the reverse.
It hides the skill from people, and makes it Claude-only.
That suits background knowledge that isn't a meaningful user action.
The exam places these two side by side, and hopes you grab the wrong one.
Now the other wrong turns.
Wrong: keep it in the personal skills folder with the right switch, and share it on a wiki.
Why?
A wiki is not distribution.
And it's never reviewed in a pull request.
Wrong: put the audit procedure into CLAUDE.md, with a line saying only run this when asked.
Why?
Three reasons.
It pays for the procedure in every session.
It can't actually stop Claude acting.
And it doesn't create a slash command at all.
A worked example from the notes pulls several fields together.
A release-candidate skill, in the project skills folder.
It has disable-model-invocation set to true, so only a human fires it.
It has narrow pre-approved tools, for git tag, git push, and opening a pull request.
And its body says: cut release candidate for the given version and target branch.
That's the shape of a well-built side-effecting procedure.
Hold on to this line. disable-model-invocation true means only a human can start it. user-invocable false means only Claude can.
Next, arguments.
Question two.
Practice question D3-008.
Here's the scenario.
A support team built a triage-ticket skill.
The frontmatter says argument-hint, with ticket-id in square brackets.
The body says: fetch ticket $ticket and classify it.
An engineer types /triage-ticket followed by the ticket number four eight two one three.
And the literal text $ticket reaches Claude, instead of the number.
What's wrong?
Take a second.
The answer. argument-hint is autocomplete text only.
Binding a named placeholder is a separate field, called arguments.
Plain version.
A form field labeled ticket number tells you what to type.
But if nobody wired that field to the system, whatever you type goes nowhere.
The label is the hint.
The wiring is what carries the value through.
In exam terms, argument-hint shows in the menu, to remind you what to type.
It never validates.
And it never binds.
The arguments field is different.
Its names map to argument positions, in order.
So setting arguments to ticket makes $ticket resolve to the first argument.
You can also use positional placeholders.
Three forms. $ARGUMENTS, for everything typed. $ARGUMENTS followed by an index, for a single position.
Or the shorthand: $0, $1, and so on.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: rewrite the hint to say required.
Why?
As if a hint could validate.
It can't, whatever you write inside it.
Wrong: add a tool pre-approval for a web-fetching command, so the skill can resolve the placeholder.
Why?
Pre-approval is about permission, not substitution.
Wrong: move the file into the commands folder, because commands bind placeholders and skills don't.
Why?
They accept the same frontmatter.
So moving the file changes packaging, not binding.
Hold on to this line. argument-hint hints. arguments binds.
Now the most misread field of all.
And it comes with the chapter's biggest source disagreement.
The field is allowed-tools.
Question three.
Practice question D3-009.
This one is pick two.
Here's the scenario.
An on-call team is writing a committed incident-snapshot skill.
It runs kubectl get commands, which read the health of containers in a Kubernetes cluster.
And it summarizes pod health for the incident channel.
Only a human may trigger it.
The kubectl get commands should not stop for approval prompts during that invocation.
And the stem is explicit: tool restrictions are already enforced separately, through the team's permission settings.
So the skill does not need to block anything.
Which two settings?
Take a second.
The answers.
First, disable-model-invocation set to true, for human-only triggering.
Second, allowed-tools set to the narrow shell rule `Bash(kubectl get *)`, with a space before the asterisk.
Here's the plain version.
A note on the counter saying use the drill without asking me today lets the handyman get on with it.
It doesn't lock the rest of the garage.
And it expires when the visit ends.
A separate house rule decides who is allowed to call the handyman in the first place.
In exam terms.
According to the notes, checked against current documentation, allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools for the turn that invokes the skill.
The grant clears when you send your next message.
And it restricts nothing.
Every other tool stays callable under your normal permission settings.
To remove tools, you use a field called disallowed-tools, or permission rules.
One more detail.
For a project skill, the grant only takes effect after the workspace trust dialog has been accepted.
Here's the disagreement.
And you must know it.
The lesson eleven slide deck describes allowed-tools as restricting which tools the skill can use.
The notes, checked against current documentation, say it only pre-approves, and restricts nothing.
For the exam, the rule is simple.
If a question frames allowed-tools as a restriction, answer in the question's own terms.
If it asks what the field actually does, pre-approval for one turn is the accurate answer.
This particular question was written to be safe either way, because it tells you the restrictions live elsewhere.
Now the wrong turns in D3-009.
Wrong: user-invocable set to false.
Why?
It has it reversed.
Wrong: `Bash(kubectl*)`, with the asterisk straight after kubectl and no space, described as blocking unlisted tools for the session.
Why?
Three errors.
The missing space widens the match.
The field blocks nothing.
And it lasts one turn, not the session.
Wrong: argument-hint, to reject invocations without a namespace.
Why?
You already know.
Hints do not validate.
Let's stay on that space for a moment.
The space before the asterisk is load-bearing in permission rule syntax.
The rule `Bash(git diff *)`, with the space, matches git diff followed by arguments.
The rule `Bash(git diff*)`, with no space, also matches other commands that merely start with those letters.
Like git diff-index.
We'll see that exact trap again in pipelines.
A follow-on from the notes.
A team wants to run their deploy tool without prompts whenever anyone is working on a release.
They propose putting it in the release skill's allowed-tools.
Does that work?
For one turn.
Then it quietly stops working.
For a session-wide or team-wide grant, put an allow rule in the permission settings.
If the whole team should have it, that's the project's .claude/settings.json.
Now a contrast segment across domains.
Three fields share almost the same name, and the exam uses them as distractors for each other.
One.
A skill's allowed-tools, here in Domain three.
It pre-approves, and restricts nothing.
Two.
A subagent's tools list, in Domain two.
It's an availability list.
A tool left out is not in that agent's session at all.
So the restriction is real.
Three.
The Agent SDK's allowed tools option, in Domain one.
It's a permission list.
That's why leaving the Agent tool out of it denies delegation.
The notes' plain version.
The skill field is a note on the counter.
The subagent field is what you put in the toolbox before handing it over.
And the SDK field is the list of what the person is permitted to use at all.
Two of the three take capability away.
The skill field is the one that doesn't.
Hold on to this line.
A skill's allowed-tools is a one-turn pre-approval that restricts nothing.
And if a question calls it a restriction, answer in the question's terms.
Last concept in this part.
Running a skill in its own space.
Question four.
Practice question D3-007.
Here's the scenario.
A research team has an evaluate-sources skill.
Its body is a list of criteria for judging source credibility.
Run inline, it floods the main conversation with dozens of file reads, across sixty collected documents.
They want the main session to receive only a findings table, with file references.
And they need that table back in the same turn.
What should they change?
Take a second.
The answer has three parts.
Add context: fork, with agent: Explore, and background: false.
And rewrite the body as an explicit task: evaluate the documents given as arguments, and return a findings table.
Here's the plain version.
Sending an assistant to the library keeps your desk clear.
But only if you tell them what to find, and what to bring back.
Hand them a page titled what makes a good source, and nothing else, and they come back empty-handed.
They never knew the question.
In exam terms.
The frontmatter setting context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent.
That subagent's prompt is the skill body.
It has no access to your conversation history.
And the main session receives only the result.
A companion field called agent picks the subagent type.
Explore, Plan, general-purpose, or a custom agent you've defined.
If you omit it, you get general-purpose.
And a forked skill runs in the background by default.
So to get the result back in the same turn, you set background: false.
Non-interactive runs, which we meet in part six, always wait.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: add fork and Explore, but leave the body as a list of criteria.
This is the trap that catches people.
Why?
A forked subagent gets the body and nothing else.
A body of pure guidelines gives it criteria, but no task.
And it returns nothing useful.
The notes call this fork-forgetting.
Wrong: keep it inline, and pre-approve read-only tools.
Why?
That moves no work out of the main context.
The reads still land there.
Wrong: keep it inline, with an argument hint for a folder.
Why?
That neither validates nor isolates anything.
Two more facts about forks from the notes.
First.
A background fork's edits fall outside session checkpoints.
So /rewind will not undo them.
Second.
If your content is reference material or conventions, rather than a task, keep it as a normal inline skill.
That already loads only when invoked, or judged relevant.
And two final frontmatter details worth recognizing.
First.
An exclamation mark followed by a command in backticks, inside the body, runs that shell command before Claude sees the skill.
And it pastes the output in.
If that command fails, the whole invocation aborts.
Second, portability.
The Agent Skills open standard defines six fields.
They are name, description, license, compatibility, metadata, and allowed-tools.
Everything else we discussed is a Claude Code extension.
And a skill uploaded to claude.ai, or through the Skills API, is rejected if it carries an extension field.
That's part two.
If you remember one thing, make it this. context: fork isolates the work.
But only a body written as a task gives the subagent something to do.
Coming up in part three: path-specific rules for conditional convention loading.
